Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Dietary vitamin D intake was not significantly associated with risk of depression in the fully adjusted model.
Sentence: "No significant association was found between vitamin D dietary intake and risk of depression in the full-adjusted model (OR: 0.96, 95% CI: 0.62, 1.51)."
Measured as: risk of depression (Beck Depression Inventory-II)
Population: 690 healthy physically active adults (athletes) aged 18-50 in Kashan, Iran
Intervention: Dietary vitamin D intake assessed by 147-item FFQ (tertiles)
Comparator: Lowest tertile of vitamin D intake
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 690
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Vitamin D deficiency was significantly associated with a current major depressive episode in pregnant women.
Sentence: "In our study, we showed a significant association between current major depressive episode in the antenatal period and vitamin D deficiency (odds ratio [OR]: 0.9; 95%CI 0.9-1.0, p = 0.003)."
Measured as: current major depressive episode in the antenatal period (MINI-Plus diagnosis)
Population: 180 pregnant women up to 24 weeks gestation (130 non-depressed, 50 depressed), Pelotas, Brazil
Intervention: Serum 25(OH)D measured by chemiluminescence (vitamin D deficiency); no intervention given
Comparator: Pregnant women without vitamin D deficiency / non-depressed women
Design: case-control study
Sample size: 180
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported
